content: The Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) has established a comprehensive framework consisting of guiding principles, goals, strategic objectives, and key actions to achieve global immunization targets. This framework is intended to guide the development of national immunization strategies, as outlined in the GVAP checklist provided in Annex 1. However, GVAP is not a detailed strategic plan in itself. Instead, it serves as a framework within which the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, and the global immunization community envision the evolution of immunization programs over the next decade. It offers a set of guiding principles and a menu of potential strategies that countries can adapt to their specific contexts when preparing their comprehensive Multi-Year Plans (cMYPs). National immunization programs have been developing strategic multi-year plans for over a decade. This guide provides an opportunity for countries to incorporate the proposed strategies and actions from the updated GVAP into their existing plans or to develop new strategic plans for their immunization programs. It is essential to align immunization programs with broader national health sector strategies, identifying clear synergies and opportunities for integration with other health programs. This alignment supports the overarching goal of reducing national morbidity and mortality rates. The national health sector plan identifies health priorities and outlines programs and strategies to achieve measurable health outcomes. Immunization programs should be integrated into the national health sector plan, as this plan forms the basis for the national health budget. The objectives, strategies, costs, and financing information from the cMYP should be incorporated into the national health plan and budget. The resources required for a National Immunization Program (NIP) are determined either within the annual budget of the Ministry of Health (MoH) or as part of a three-year rolling Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF). Since government funding may come from both central and sub-national sources, the cMYP must account for sub-national budgets, costs, expenditures, and priorities. Analyzing costs and projecting budgets at the sub-national level is particularly important in countries where decentralization has shifted decision-making and resource allocation to local government authorities. The relationships between immunization program planning, budgeting/financing processes, and overall national processes are illustrated in Figure 4. On the planning side, the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and National Development Plans provide a framework for generating the overall health sector plan, of which the cMYP is a part. On the budgeting and financing side, external partner funding may be channeled through the investment budget (as extra-budgetary) or combined with recurrent government funding (through budget support or basket funding for sector-wide approaches, or SWAps). The cMYP costing tool can be used to capture and allocate immunization expenditures within these frameworks. When developing the cMYP, it is beneficial to identify potential linkages with other health interventions to achieve national health goals more effectively. For example, combining immunization with interventions such as vitamin A supplementation, distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets for malaria prevention, and anti-helminthic treatments for soil-transmitted helminths can yield significant benefits. Some vaccines, such as pneumococcal, rotavirus, or human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines, require supplementary approaches to achieve comprehensive control of pneumonia, diarrhea, and cervical cancer. Planning for such linkages may involve reviewing other health program plans, such as those for integrated management of neonatal and childhood illnesses (IMNCI), malaria, nutrition, and non-communicable disease (NCD) control, to identify areas of synergy. Regular discussions can then determine the best strategies to adopt and plan activities for training, service delivery, and monitoring. Many countries have developed essential medical care benefit packages that include immunization and other maternal and child health-care interventions delivered either at fixed health facilities or through outreach services. Integrating programs through common delivery systems promotes efficiency by sharing costs and, most importantly, enhances impact by making more life-saving interventions accessible to the population. The cMYP costing tool can be used to capture and allocate the immunization portion of expenditures in such settings. The development, implementation, and monitoring of the cMYP follow a sequential process. This process begins with convening meetings of all key immunization stakeholders, including those at the sub-national level, to identify linkages and coordinate and integrate all aspects of the national program into a single planning process. This includes components such as polio, measles, maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT), new vaccines, logistics, routine immunization, surveillance, communicable disease control, laboratory services, health planning, health economics, budgeting, communication, and social mobilization. Representatives from the Ministry of Finance (MoF), Ministry of Budget, and local governments responsible for health sector financing should also be included. Participants should be briefed on findings from recent immunization reviews and studies, including Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) reviews, coverage surveys, cold-chain assessments, recommendations from the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG), data-quality assessments, and other studies. They should also be informed about the seven immunization components and the steps in the planning process. Previously separate plans for polio, measles, cold-chain, and maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) must be fully incorporated into the cMYP and linked to other health interventions. Additionally, the costs of campaigns, routine programs, and training must be included in the costing and financing process of the cMYP. All stakeholders must arrive at a common vision of national program priorities and strategic direction. Following this, the interagency coordinating committee (ICC) or health sector steering committee (HSSC) or other relevant stakeholders should convene. Involving a broader group of stakeholders is crucial to ensure that all activities, including accelerated disease control activities, are articulated from the outset; facilitate the linkage between the cMYP annual plans and budgets to sector and national budgets and plans; advocate for the immunization program as a means to achieve the Child Health MDG (MDG 4); capture all external and government financial flows to the NIP; and mobilize the resources needed to reduce or eliminate financing gaps. In most countries, the ICC meeting is the most relevant venue for discussions with all partners. However, in some countries, it may be more appropriate to work with sector coordinating bodies such as SWAp health partners. At some point, the same state actors identified in the first step should be brought together with ICC representatives, as the cMYP includes assessments of past expenditures and future program financing from all sources. Elected leaders, health sector and Ministry of Finance officials, civil society, private sector, and academic representatives should also be consulted and involved. Elected leaders play a critical role in fostering political commitment to the program's goals. Their engagement is essential not only for resource mobilization but also for enacting laws and regulations to ensure sustainable public financing. Civil society adds value to the cMYP by giving voice to non-state actors, including socially and economically disadvantaged groups such as ethnic minorities or the urban poor, and by collaborating with other agencies to extend health-care services to populations in conflict or post-conflict settings. Civil society can also advocate for increased national funding for immunization and work with communities on vaccine acceptance. The private medical, supply chain, and equipment maintenance sectors are important for ensuring high-quality services. Academic institutions should be engaged to strengthen the research and evaluation components of the program. Many of these stakeholders can contribute to immunization policy and planning decision-making through representation in National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and their respective secretariats. The cMYP development process involves several steps, including conducting a situation analysis, determining national priorities, setting objectives and milestones, planning strategies and key activities, reviewing planned activities against GVAP and health sector strategies, creating an activity timeline, analyzing costs and financing gaps, and mobilizing resources. The final steps include putting the cMYP into action, monitoring, and evaluating its implementation.
